source: MIT 14.01 Principles of Microeconomics, Lecture 1, ~22-30 min
keypoints: Someone auctioned a kidney on eBay with bidding starting at $25,000; bidding reached $5 million before eBay shut it down.
The positive question is 'Why did the price get so high?', answerable with the supply and demand model alone.
The kidney price soared because demand is extremely high (people pay everything to live) and legal supply is extremely low.
The normative question is 'Should we be allowed to sell our bodily organs?', which is fundamentally an economics question.
Many Americans die because the supply of organs cannot meet the demand from those with organ failure.
The standard economic argument for organ sales: a person with two healthy kidneys can function fine with one and use the money to transform their family's life.
For about the first 11 lectures of the course, the free market is treated as king.
The lecturer describes economics as fundamentally a right-wing science: the market knows best.
There are only two reasons to interfere with the market, and the first is market failure: the market not working properly.
Market-failure concerns in organ sales include coercion (people forcing their children), criminal activity, and sellers not understanding the danger.
About 100,000 Americans currently live with hepatitis C, which causes kidney failure and can lie dormant for years, so a seller might unknowingly be at risk.
The black market is not itself a market failure: economists simply view it as another market.
